sections.overview: The emu is Australia’s tallest native bird, a flightless runner living across much of the mainland. Rainfall shapes its movements and breeding opportunities. A distinctive feature of its life cycle is male-only incubation and care of striped, mobile chicks.
sections.identification: Adults stand 1.6–1.9 m, with shaggy grey-brown feathers, a sparsely feathered bluish head and neck, tiny wings and long legs. Each foot has three forward toes; ostriches are taller and have two. Chicks bear dark stripes. Adult mass is about 30–45 kg; the consulted sources do not give a dependable sex-specific adult mass range.
sections.habitat: Emus range across mainland Australia, from coastal regions and woodlands to open plains. They avoid rainforest and very arid areas. Where food or water varies, birds move in response to climate and rainfall, sometimes hundreds of kilometres.
sections.diet: They eat nutrient-rich fruits, seeds, flowers and young shoots, plus insects and small animals when available. Food changes seasonally with plant growth and rain; swallowed pebbles help the gizzard grind it. They generally avoid dry grass and mature leaves.
sections.behavior: Usually seen alone, in pairs or loose groups, emus make low booming, drumming and grunting calls using a tracheal pouch. Strong legs support rapid running, zigzag escape from aerial predators and defensive kicks at close range.
sections.reproduction: Breeding often occurs in late autumn and winter, but varies regionally. The pair makes a shallow ground nest; after laying dark-green eggs, the female usually leaves. The male fasts while incubating for about eight weeks, then guards and accompanies striped chicks for months. They walk and forage soon after hatching.
sections.ecology: On the NSW north coast, emus disperse native plant seeds over long distances; chicks also eat caterpillars and grasshoppers. Their movements between feeding and nesting sites require connected habitat. Roads, fences and land conversion can block travel or kill birds.
sections.conservation: The species remains widespread on mainland Australia, but some local populations are declining. A 2020 NSW profile classifies the north-coast and Port Stephens population as endangered, citing habitat loss and fragmentation, altered fire, predators, traffic and barriers. This regional status does not establish a global category.
